items.title: Ken Peplowski interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 9, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: I played in Loren Schoenberg’s band, a great guy who now is up at the Jazz Museum in Harlem. He had a wonderful big band. And we had kind of semi-regular gigs with that band.

ctx.x: 1997. We had just sort of started doing these interview sessions and I remember that was, musically that was a great party. I wonder if you could do me a favor, for people who will watch this and if you can think back to 1997 or about then, what a typical, let’s say week or ten day period for you was like, employment/music-wise.

Yeah. That, you know the 80s and 90s were really interesting for me ‘cause there were a lot of different kinds of gigs that I did, everything from big bands, small groups, there were a lot of big bands still playing in New York. I played in Loren Schoenberg’s band, a great guy who now is up at the Jazz Museum in Harlem. He had a wonderful big band. And we had kind of semi-regular gigs with that band. Mel Lewis was the drummer. And I was recording for Concord at that time, traveling quite a bit which I still am,…

items.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019
items.q: my sax section was already set — it was set for a while. Chuck Wilson and Jack Stooky on altos, Ken Peplowski and Doug Lawrence on tenors, and Danny Bank.

ctx.x: You’ve got to have a doctorate to do anything. But anyway, I left school and went to work for Benny Goodman. And he was paying me I think it was $250 a week to come in and my job was to say — you know to have a stack of arrangements and you would say now there’s three versions of the “King Porter Stomp” here. Now one’s in — two are in D flat, there’s one in G, and this one has Fletcher Henderson’s name on it but this one doesn’t but it says Ziggy on the trumpet part or something like that. And so I mean it was…

to play if you loved swing music and loved big band music, the only way to play it in 1979 or ’80 for a young musician was in these kind of like second rate bands that played stock arrangements or transcriptions and you might have three or four really great players in the band and some others that weren’t so great. It was a lot of fun and it paid. But it was not at all excellent playing. So one of those bands was a band led by a guy named Bob January. And the singer in his band was Barbara Lea. And we became…
